title: Accelerator
source: The Founding and Manifesto of Futurism
author: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti
idea: A drum machine that can only speed up, until it crashes and starts again.
controls: The tempo climbs on its own; ACCEL sets how hard you press the pedal and BRAKE (or B) drops it back. Click the squares to change the pistons (kick, snare, hat).

title: Intonarumori
source: The Art of Noises (L'arte dei rumori)
author: Luigi Russolo
idea: Six noise machines, one for each of Russolo's six families of noise, cranked by hand.
controls: Each column is one family of noise. Drag up and down inside a column to crank its pitch, click its name to switch it on or off, and click the dots to change its rhythm.

title: Enharmonic
source: Manifesto of Futurist Musicians
author: Francesco Balilla Pratella
idea: A quarter-tone melody machine in free metre, where every bar chooses its own length.
controls: Each block in the chain is one bar and its width is its number of beats. ENHARMONIC moves from ordinary semitones to quarter tones and free microtones.

title: Cut-up Hat
source: Dada Manifesto 1918
author: Tristan Tzara
idea: Your loop is cut into words, shaken in a hat and played back in the order the pieces come out.
controls: The loop is cut into slices and each slice gets a newspaper word. SHAKE THE HAT draws a new order, which then repeats faithfully, as Tzara's recipe says.

title: Automatic
source: Manifesto of Surrealism
author: André Breton
idea: Draw without stopping to think: your hand becomes a melody and an exquisite corpse in three parts.
controls: Drag inside one of the three panels (head, body, legs) and keep moving: height sets the pitch, left to right scrubs through your sample, and speed sets the volume. Let go and the drawing loops for ever.

title: Neo-Plastic Grid
source: De Stijl Manifesto I
author: Theo van Doesburg, Piet Mondrian, Vilmos Huszár, Antony Kok and others
idea: A Mondrian composition you can hear: vertical lines are time, horizontal lines are pitch, colours are instruments.
controls: The playhead sweeps left to right. Each coloured rectangle sounds when the playhead reaches it and lasts as long as it is wide.

title: Building
source: Programme of the Staatliches Bauhaus in Weimar
author: Walter Gropius
idea: Build a song floor by floor from Bauhaus shapes: blue circles, red squares, yellow triangles.
controls: The music climbs the building from the ground floor up, one floor per bar, and each floor has four beats. Click a cell to place a shape: ● blue circle plays a bass and fifth, ■ red square plays a slice of your sample, ▲ yellow triangle plays quick metal hits.

title: Kinetic Rhythms
source: The Realistic Manifesto
author: Naum Gabo and Antoine Pevsner
idea: Three rotating rods sweep through points in space; every crossing is a note, so rhythm comes from motion, not mass.
controls: Three rods turn at different speeds. Click anywhere in the circle to add a point and shift-click (or right-click) to remove one.

title: Zero of Form
source: From Cubism and Futurism to Suprematism: The New Painterly Realism
author: Kazimir Malevich
idea: Pure shapes float on white; each one is a held tone, and where they overlap your sample sparkles.
controls: Every shape is a sustained sound: height is pitch, size is loudness, and the kind of shape sets the timbre (square: pure tone, bar: reedy, circle: your sample looped, cross: noise). Drag shapes to move them and double-click empty white to add a new one.

title: Zaum
source: A Slap in the Face of Public Taste
author: David Burliuk, Aleksei Kruchenykh, Vladimir Mayakovsky and Velimir Khlebnikov
idea: Type words that mean nothing in any language and a throat made of your sample sings them.
controls: The words in the megaphone are sung syllable by syllable: vowels are sung through vocal formant filters, and consonants become hisses, clicks, trills and hums. Type your own transrational words, or press INVENT for new ones (or ask Gemini, if you have a key).

title: Theory of Intervals
source: WE: Variant of a Manifesto
author: Dziga Vertov (the Kinoks group)
idea: A film strip of sample 'shots', where the loudest music happens in the cuts between them.
controls: Each frame on the strip is a shot: a piece of your sample with its own speed and length. Between shots is an interval, and it sounds as a sweep from one shot to the next, bigger when the shots are more different.

title: BLAST / BLESS
source: BLAST, Manifesto of the Vorticists
author: Wyndham Lewis, with Ezra Pound, Gaudier-Brzeska and others
idea: Every instrument is a word on the wall: BLAST it and it hits hard and dirty, BLESS it and it turns soft and holy.
controls: Click a word to cycle it: off, then BLAST (loud, distorted, short), then BLESS (gentle, sustained, reverberant). Your sample is the word SAMPLE.

title: Event Scores
source: Fluxus Manifesto
author: George Maciunas
idea: A deck of Fluxus-style instruction cards; the machine performs whichever card is on top, then flips the next.
controls: The top card is performed for about eight seconds, then the next card is drawn. Each card is a tiny instruction (drip, repeat, count, stretch, swarm, hold, reverse, silence) carried out on your sample.

title: Dérive
source: Report on the Construction of Situations
author: Guy Debord
idea: A walker drifts through a psychogeographic city; each district has its own sound, and the city's pull decides the route.
controls: The walker drifts through the city map, pulled by the districts and by chance. Your footsteps are tiny grains of your sample.

title: Painted Lines
source: The Stuckists manifesto
author: Billy Childish and Charles Thomson
idea: Paint melodies by hand in screen-print layers; the loop prints one colour at a time, then all of them together.
controls: Pick an ink, then paint on the sheet: left to right is time and height is pitch. Each ink is a voice and plays a continuous gliding line wherever you painted: pink is your sample, sung; yellow is a pure lead; blue is the bass; green is a brushed noise.

title: Vow of Chastity
source: Dogme 95 Manifesto and Vow of Chastity
author: Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg
idea: One sample, no effects, no grid: you play it live by hand, and every rule you break goes in a public confession.
controls: A take loops for four bars. Press the keys A S D F G H J K (or click the pads) to play your sample from eight cue points, live, with handheld timing wobble.

title: Credo
source: The Future of Music: Credo
author: John Cage
idea: Three coins tossed six times build an I Ching hexagram, and the hexagram picks the sound, its length and its loudness from a chart.
controls: For each event the machine tosses three coins six times to build a hexagram (1 to 64), which picks one of 64 sounds from the chart (slices of your sample, tones, noises and silences). Two more hexagrams pick its duration and its dynamics.

title: Breath Squares
source: Sonic Meditations
author: Pauline Oliveros
idea: Four nested squares are four drones that breathe; colours that sit close together make their tones beat against each other.
controls: Press PLAY and listen. The squares breathe on their own, slowly.

title: BECAUSE
source: Riot Grrrl Manifesto
author: Kathleen Hanna (with Bikini Kill)
idea: A three-chord punk machine where your BECAUSE lines become the riffs and the shouted rhythm.
controls: Write your own BECAUSE lines. Each line is one section of the song: the number of letters in each word picks the chord (only three chords, I, IV and V, are allowed), and the syllables are shouted in rhythm using your sample as the voice.

title: Cyborg
source: A Cyborg Manifesto
author: Donna Haraway
idea: Three boundary sliders (human/animal, organism/machine, physical/non-physical) blur one groove between flesh and code.
controls: A groove plays, built from your sample. Drag the three sliders to break three boundaries.

title: Virus Matrix
source: A Cyberfeminist Manifesto for the 21st Century
author: VNS Matrix (collective)
idea: A step grid that is also a living culture: a virus spreads through the pattern each cycle, corrupting the notes it touches.
controls: Each column is a step and each row is a slice of your sample. Pink cells are healthy notes; green cells are the virus, which plays a mutated, crushed and reversed version of the sound.

title: Change Nature
source: Xenofeminism: A Politics for Alienation
author: Laboria Cuboniks (collective)
idea: The harmonic 'laws' of music are editable: choose the octave, the number of notes in it and how the overtones stretch.
controls: A chord machine plays a progression. Nothing about the tuning is fixed: EDO sets how many equal steps divide the octave (12 is normal; try 5, 7, 19, 22 or 31).

title: Auto-Destructive Loop
source: Auto-Destructive Art (manifestos 1 to 3)
author: Gustav Metzger
idea: A loop that destroys itself as it plays; its slow death is the piece, shown as a wall of bananas turning from green to brown.
controls: Your sample loops in 48 pieces, one banana per piece. Every pass, acid eats into the loop: pieces fade, crackle, drop out and at last fall silent, and their bananas ripen and rot.

title: Art Concret
source: The Basis of Concrete Painting (Art Concret)
author: Theo van Doesburg, Otto G. Carlsund, Jean Hélion, Léon Tutundjian and Marcel Wantz
idea: Every voice is a written formula, step × a + b mod n, so the whole piece is constructed in the mind before a sound is made.
controls: Each of the six rows is a voice defined by four whole numbers. A step sounds when (step × a + b) mod n is less than k.

title: Spatial Cuts
source: Manifiesto Blanco (White Manifesto)
author: Lucio Fontana, with students at the Academia Altamira
idea: A painted drone is the canvas; slash it, and each cut opens a window through which your sample comes from the space behind.
controls: Press PLAY to hear the canvas, a flat coloured drone. Drag across the canvas to slash it.

title: Matter Alive
source: Gutai Art Manifesto
author: Jirō Yoshihara
idea: Your sample is the ground: throw balls of mud, paint and paper onto its waveform, and every impact plays the sound at that spot.
controls: The landscape is the waveform of your sample. Click or drag anywhere to throw material onto it (choose MUD, PAINT or PAPER).

title: Bicho
source: Neo-Concrete Manifesto
author: Ferreira Gullar, with Amilcar de Castro, Lygia Clark, Lygia Pape, Franz Weissmann, Reynaldo Jardim and Theon Spanúdis
idea: A hinged metal creature: bend its plates and the angles between them become the intervals of its chord.
controls: The creature is five plates joined by hinges. Drag any plate to fold it around its hinge.

title: Anthropophagy
source: Manifesto Antropófago (Cannibal Manifesto)
author: Oswald de Andrade
idea: Feed the mouth sounds from anywhere; it chews them into pieces and digests them into a new Brazilian rhythm.
controls: The mouth eats sounds: every sample you load is eaten, and so are the built-in sounds (click FEED to give it another). It chews each sound into pieces that go into the stomach.

title: Ultra Metaphor
source: Ultraísmo
author: Jorge Luis Borges
idea: Fuse two sound images into one metaphor: the rhythm of one drives the body of the other, with every ornament stripped away.
controls: Pick a first image (its rhythm and gesture) and a second image (its body and colour). The machine fuses them into one metaphor, so 'the train is a bird' plays bird chirps in the rhythm of a train.

title: Strident Radio
source: Actual No. 1 (Comprimido estridentista)
author: Manuel Maples Arce
idea: Tune a wireless dial across a 1920s city: every station is a different broadcast of your sample, with static and howl in between.
controls: Drag the dial, or use the arrow keys, to tune between seven stations. Each station broadcasts your sample in a different way (a jazz band, a factory, the news in Morse, a tango orchestra, a choir and a strident siren).

title: Zenith
source: Manifesto of Zenitism
author: Ljubomir Micić
idea: An endless climb to the zenith: Shepard tones and a sample that rises forever but never arrives.
controls: Every voice climbs, and as each one gets too high it fades out while a new one fades in at the bottom, so the climb never ends (a Shepard–Risset glissando). Your sample rises with the tones, re-pitched in ever-higher layers.

title: Make It Bloom
source: Non serviam and Creacionismo
author: Vicente Huidobro
idea: Don't sing the rose, make it bloom: build a new sound from nothing, partial by partial, then let it flower through your sample.
controls: Draw on the sixteen bars to build a new sound from its harmonics (partials). Each column is one partial, from the fundamental on the left upward.

title: Slow Cooker
source: Slow Food Manifesto
author: Folco Portinari, for the movement founded by Carlo Petrini
idea: Time-stretch your sample until it slows to near stillness, simmering it in grains that you season and leave to ripen.
controls: Your sample is put in the pot and played back extremely slowly as a cloud of grains (up to 200 times slower) without changing its pitch. SLOWNESS sets how slowly the cooking head moves through the sound.

title: Repurpose Platform
source: #Accelerate: Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics
author: Alex Williams and Nick Srnicek
idea: Steer a vector between four futures and repurpose the machine itself: every corner is a whole groove, and you can always expand the map.
controls: Drag the cursor around the square. Each corner is a complete groove (FOLK LOOP, FACTORY, NETWORK and POST-WORK) and the music is a weighted blend of all four, recalculated every step.

title: Airport Loops
source: Ambient Music (liner notes to Ambient 1: Music for Airports)
author: Brian Eno
idea: Seven loops of different, unrelated lengths drift in and out of phase, so the music never repeats in the same way.
controls: Each ring is a tape loop with its own length in seconds (for example 17.8, 20.1, 31.8). Each loop carries a single note or your sample (loaded sounds enter on their loops straight away), and because the lengths share no common measure, the combinations never repeat exactly.

title: Idea Machine
source: Paragraphs on Conceptual Art
author: Sol LeWitt
idea: Write wall-drawing instructions and the machine executes them blindly: each line drawn across the grid becomes a melody.
controls: The list on the right is a set of instructions in the style of a wall drawing ('5 straight lines from the left edge to the right edge, in blue'). The machine carries them out on a 16 × 12 grid.

title: No
source: No Manifesto
author: Yvonne Rainer
idea: A full, flashy groove that you take apart with thirteen NOs, until only an ordinary walking pulse is left.
controls: The groove starts with everything: echo and reverb, fast fills, filter sweeps, a star lead, heroic chords, swing and moving pans. Each line on the right is one NO from the manifesto.

title: Maintenance
source: Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969! Proposal for an exhibition 'CARE'
author: Mierle Laderman Ukeles
idea: The music gets dirty and falls apart on its own; your job is to look after it, and the care itself becomes the rhythm.
controls: Four tracks play (DRUMS, BASS, CHORDS and your SAMPLE). Left alone they gather dust: notes drop out, the pitch sags, hiss builds up and the timing wanders.

title: Mould
source: Mould Manifesto against Rationalism in Architecture (Verschimmelungsmanifest)
author: Friedensreich Hundertwasser
idea: A rigid, straight step grid is slowly overgrown by mould, and wherever the mould spreads, the notes bend, drift and grow organic.
controls: The sequencer starts as a strict rectilinear grid of notes, perfectly straight and in time. Mould grows over it by itself, cell by cell.

title: Ornament & Crime
source: Ornament and Crime (Ornament und Verbrechen)
author: Adolf Loos
idea: Decorate a plain melody with trills, turns and grace notes, but every ornament costs labour, and the bill and the fashion clock are always running.
controls: A plain melody (your sample sings the main notes) loops over eight steps. Click a note to cycle its ornament: none, grace note, mordent, turn and trill.

title: The Store
source: I am for an art...
author: Claes Oldenburg
idea: A corner shop of found sounds: every product on the shelves is a sound object, and whatever you put in your basket becomes the song.
controls: The shelves are stocked with sound products (cut from your sample and from built-in sounds), each with a price tag and a kind (THUMP, CLICK, HUM, VOICE, FIZZ or JINGLE). Click a product to add it to your basket.

title: Scratch Orchestra
source: A Scratch Orchestra: draft constitution
author: Cornelius Cardew
idea: A crowd of amateur players, each with their own scratch music, performing a sequence of rites chosen from the orchestra's constitution.
controls: Each circle is a player with their own little ostinato (their 'scratch music'), instrument and favourite note. Players come and go: ADD PLAYER recruits one more, click a player to send them home.

title: Für Statik
source: Für Statik (For Statics)
author: Jean Tinguely
idea: A rickety machine of meshing gears: each gear's teeth strike notes, so the gear ratios become polyrhythms, and the machine wobbles because nothing stays still.
controls: The motor (red) drives a chain of meshing gears. A gear with more teeth turns more slowly, so the ratios between gears create polyrhythms.

title: Décollage
source: Nouveau Réalisme manifestos
author: Pierre Restany
idea: Three posters pasted on top of each other, each one a different groove; tear strips away to reveal the layers underneath.
controls: The wall has three posters pasted on top of each other. Each poster is a complete loop, from the top layer (a brass-band march) down to a jazz layer and finally your sample, pasted first on the bare wall.

title: Poor Means
source: Arte Povera: Notes for a Guerrilla War
author: Germano Celant
idea: Four poor materials (wire, stone, water and rag) and only the energy of your hands: pluck, strike, drip and rub.
controls: The table has four poor materials. WIRE: drag across the wires to pluck them (a physically modelled string, tuned by its length).

title: Databend
source: Glitch Studies Manifesto
author: Rosa Menkman
idea: Bend the raw data of your sample: shift its bytes, flip its bits, swap and repeat its blocks, and listen to the medium break open.
controls: Your sample is turned into raw data (bytes) and played back as a loop. Each operation edits that data directly, as if you had opened the file in a text editor: SHIFT (moves the byte alignment, so the samples are read wrongly), FLIP (inverts random bits), SWAP (exchanges two blocks), STUTTER (repeats a block), 8-BIT (reads it as cheap 8-bit audio) and ZERO (wipes a block).

title: Sound Masses
source: The Liberation of Sound
author: Edgard Varèse
idea: Three sirens and colliding sound masses: drag the sirens' pitch planes through space, and where they meet, the masses penetrate or repel.
controls: Each coloured plane is a sound mass driven by a siren (a continuously gliding tone) with a beating cluster around it. Drag the planes up and down (pitch) and left and right (space: pan).

title: Constellation
source: From Line to Constellation (vom vers zur konstellation)
author: Eugen Gomringer
idea: Place a few words on the page like stars: their positions make the rhythm and space, and their letters make the melody.
controls: Each word is a star in a constellation. A slow sweep moves from left to right, and when it reaches a word, the word is sung: each letter is a note (vowels are long and consonants are short, struck with your sample), its height is the pitch register and its size is the loudness.

title: Letter Drum
source: Lettrism: Manifesto of Lettrist Poetry
author: Isidore Isou
idea: A drum machine made of letters: type a line and every character is a percussive phoneme, including Isou's new letters for breaths, clicks, whistles and kisses.
controls: Type into the line (up to 32 characters); each character is one step. Vowels are sung vowel sounds, consonants are percussive (K, T, P and similar are hard hits; S, F, SH and similar are noise; M, N and L are hums), and your sample speaks the capital letters.

title: Ecstatic Truth
source: Minnesota Declaration: Truth and Fact in Documentary Cinema
author: Werner Herzog
idea: One slider from the accountant's truth to ecstatic truth: the same recording, played plainly as fact or stylised, slowed and staged into something deeper.
controls: Your sample is the 'footage'. With the slider at FACT, it plays exactly as recorded, cut on a strict grid, with a dry log of the facts (times, levels).

title: Both-And
source: Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (Nonstraightforward Architecture: A Gentle Manifesto)
author: Robert Venturi
idea: A machine that refuses to choose: every musical decision is a pair of opposites, and in the middle you get both at once. Major and minor, four and three, clean and dirty, straight and swung.
controls: Each of the four big striped sliders is a contradiction. Push it left for one side, right for the other, or leave it in the middle to hear BOTH, which is where Venturi says the life is.

title: Actual Life Journal
source: Found-sound production: the voice-memo diary method
author: Fred again..
idea: A diary you can dance to: a voice memo is chopped into emotional vocal hooks, laid over a field recording and house or two-step garage drums, and taken through intro, build, drop and break.
controls: 6 slots (voice memo, field recording, keys, kick, clap, hats); chop grid with per-step pitch; 3 drum styles with swing; 6 chord progressions in any key; field-bed level and sidechain pump; auto-arranged or hand-played INTRO/BUILD/DROP/BREAK with hold-to-build; Gemini turns a description of your day into an arrangement.

title: Seed Garden
source: Generative systems: tape loops, gardening and oblique prompts
author: Brian Eno, with Peter Schmidt for Oblique Strategies
idea: Plant sounds as tape loops of different lengths and let them drift in and out of phase, so the music is never the same twice. Garden it with seeds, pruning, weather, a deck of oblique prompt cards and a tape machine that prints the garden back into itself.
controls: 6 slots (piano, voice, texture, bell, found sound, TAPE); up to 12 loop beds, each with its own length, note, sound, swell and pan; scale, key, octave and loop-length programme; attention slider (ignorable to interesting); growth and weather; Discreet-style tape echo with wow and hiss; oblique prompt cards that really change the system; PRINT TO TAPE resampling; a Gerstner morphological box that writes a whole programme.

title: Gradual Process
source: Music as a Gradual Process
author: Steve Reich
idea: Set a process going and listen to it run: copies of one pattern drift out of phase (Piano Phase, It's Gonna Rain), fill in note by note (Drumming) or stretch out (Four Organs), and new patterns appear from the gaps.
controls: 4 slots (two keyboard voices, a tape loop and a pulse); 4 processes (phase, tape phase, additive build, augmentation); 2 to 4 voices with their own slot, octave and pan; editable 4 to 16 step pattern on a scale grid in any key; continuous or step-wise phasing with drift and hold; build and augmentation rates; chain processes; MIDI transposes.

title: Murmuration
source: Emergence: the murmuration
author: Craig Reynolds (1987); Ballerini, Cabibbo, Parisi and colleagues, STARFLAG (2008)
idea: No bird leads a murmuration. Each one follows three local rules and watches about seven neighbours, and the shape of the whole flock comes out of that. Here each bird is also a sound: its height sets the pitch, its heading picks the point in your sample, and its speed sets the level.
controls: 4 species slots (chatter, wings, wind and call) with a mix for each; flock size; Reynolds's separation, alignment and cohesion; topological (k nearest) or metric neighbours; speed, wander and wind; a predator under the mouse with strength; grain rate, length, scale, key and range; wing-wash level; MIDI notes release a flock in that key.

title: The Colour Keyboard
source: Concerning the Spiritual in Art
author: Wassily Kandinsky (1866 to 1944)
idea: Kandinsky said colour is a keyboard and the soul is the piano. Paint a composition from points, lines, triangles, squares and circles, and a playhead plays it: the colour picks the instrument (yellow is a trumpet, blue a cello), the shape sets how each note is played, and white and black are two kinds of silence.
controls: 6 colour slots (yellow, red, blue, green, orange, violet) for your own sounds; 5 shapes (point, line glissando, triangle, square, circle); size, height and rotation; white (a pause) and black (cuts everything); loop length, tempo, scale, key and range; snap to grid; scan or radial reading; undo and clear; a COMPOSE generator; Gemini paints a composition from a mood; MIDI plays the colours live.

title: Live Live
source: Found-sound production: a live set from one pad sampler
author: Fred again..
idea: Play a whole set from one pad sampler, in the style of a famous 2022 club-stream set played live from one sampler: sixteen pads in four banks (one phrase chopped or re-pitched into a melody, drums, chords, effects), a pattern recorder to build the track live from scratch, a CDJ deck underneath, and a held build that drops after a beat of silence.
controls: 7 slots (phrase, keys, kick, clap, hats, CDJ track, field); 4 banks of 16 pads with per-pad pitch, gain, length and pan; phrase chopped at word onsets or equally, or one chop re-pitched across the pads in any key and scale; choke; note repeat (1/8, 1/16, 1/32); quantised overdub pattern recorder (1, 2 or 4 bars) with an editable roll; 4 grooves (house, UK garage 2-step, breakbeat, half-time) with swing and sidechain pump; CDJ deck that locks a loop to tempo, with stop and tape stop; hold-to-build with snare roll, riser and high-pass, gap and drop; FROM SCRATCH autopilot that adds layers in order; MIDI pads on notes 36 to 51.

title: Endless Music Box
source: Generative systems: Bloom, an endless music machine
author: Brian Eno and Peter Chilvers
idea: A playable generative instrument inspired by the generative app Bloom (2008): tap and each note blooms, comes back every cycle a little quieter and slowly drifts, and when you stop playing the music box carries on by itself, over a slowly recombining painting of colour fields.
controls: 5 slots (glass, piano, voice, drone, painting texture); 12 moods (key, scale, sounds and colours) with shuffle; cycle length and a second, out-of-step cycle for the right half; decay per repeat or FREEZE; drift (repeats wander to neighbouring notes); chord taps; range and brightness; evolve-when-idle with its own wait and density; drone and painting layers; echo and reverb; MIDI notes plant notes.

title: Closed Groove
source: Musique concrète and the sound object
author: Pierre Schaeffer (1910 to 1995), with Pierre Henry and the Groupe de Recherche de Musique Concrète
idea: Pierre Schaeffer's musique concrète as a four-turntable instrument: cut any sound into eight sound objects, label each one with a simplified version of his typology, then loop them in closed grooves, slow them down, cut off their attacks and reverse them, the way the Étude aux chemins de fer was made from railway recordings in 1948.
controls: 4 source slots (railway, bell, voice, tone) cut into 4 to 8 objects at onsets or equally; per-turntable source, object, hit or closed-groove mode, speed, attack cut, length, reverse, level, pan, tone, space and a 16-step pattern; tempo and swing; acousmatic (reduced listening) mode; automatic étude; spatial relief.

title: Golden Angle
source: Phyllotaxis: the golden angle and the sunflower
author: H. Vogel; Stéphane Douady and Yves Couder; Alan Turing; D'Arcy Thompson
idea: A sunflower head as a sequencer: seeds are born one by one, each turned 137.5° from the last (the golden angle), as in H. Vogel's 1979 model of phyllotaxis. Every birth is a note, a rotating arm plays the seeds it passes, and a Fibonacci-word rhythm ticks underneath. Change the angle and you can hear (and see) why plants pick the irrational one.
controls: 5 slots (seed, petal, bell, drone, pulse); divergence angle with golden, Lucas and rational presets; birth rate, maximum seeds and what happens when the head is full; 1, 2, 3 or 5 arms, sweep speed, listening band and quantise; pitch from spiral family (n mod 8, 13, 21 or 34) or from radius; key, scale and octaves; Fibonacci-word rhythm of length 8, 13, 21 or 34; spiral overlay; drone, swing and space.

title: Rayonist Rays
source: Rayonists and Futurists: A Manifesto
author: Mikhail Larionov (1881 to 1964) and Natalia Goncharova (1881 to 1962), signed with other Moscow artists
idea: The Rayonist manifesto of 1913 made playable: objects send out coloured rays, which reflect off the edges, and music happens only where rays cross. A scan line reads the intersections from left to right like a score, so the forms made where reflected rays meet are what you hear.
controls: 5 slots (four ray timbres and an object hum); drag, add or delete objects and give each one a timbre, a ray count and a spin; rays, fan spread, length, rotation and edge reflection; 'objects don't matter' mode; scan length, notes per step, key, scale and octaves; Futurist motor (kick and hats), swing, echo and space; optional Gemini that turns a scene you describe into objects.

title: Spoken Mantra
source: Found-sound production: found speech as the song
author: Fred again.., with The Blessed Madonna
idea: A spoken sentence, not a sung one, becomes the whole song, the found-speech method: a few words of a real person talking, repeated until they become the hook. The speech is cut into words, you choose which words make the mantra, a piano listens to the pitch of each word and harmonises it, and the arrangement runs intro, mantra, build (the phrase shrinks to one stuttering word), a beat of silence, then a pumping house or two-step drop.
controls: 6 slots (speech, piano, kick, clap, hats, field recording); click words to build the mantra; word chopping by gaps or equal slices; phrase timing natural or quantised; key, mode and progression or 'follow the speech'; groove (house, two-step, half-time, none), sidechain pump, hook density and re-pitched hooks; section lengths, auto-arrange or play sections by hand with a held build; riser, echo and space; optional Gemini that turns a moment you describe into an arrangement.

title: Discreet System
source: Generative systems: Discreet Music, a system set going
author: Brian Eno; B side performed by the Cockpit Ensemble, conducted by Gavin Bryars
design_credit: Isotype (Otto Neurath, Marie Neurath and Gerd Arntz)
idea: Discreet Music (1975) as an instrument you set going and then leave alone: two short melodies of different lengths feed a graphic equaliser and a long tape-delay loop of two tape machines, so every note comes back, quieter and darker, for minutes. Draw the EQ, let it drift, turn the listening level down to the edge of hearing, like a record left playing too quietly in one speaker, and bring in canon players who each slow down at a different rate.
controls: 4 slots (line A, line B, canon players, room tone); two (or three) melodies with their own note counts and lengths, drawn on a grid; key and scale; tape delay time, feedback, wow, tape tone and saturation, a short echo; an 8-band graphic EQ you draw, with optional slow drift; listening level and a one-speaker 'harp record' mode; Pachelbel canon players with tempo spread; tempo and space.

title: Row Matrix
source: Composition with twelve tones related only with one another
author: Arnold Schoenberg (1874 to 1951)
year: 1923 (first wholly twelve-tone pieces, the Piano Suite Op. 25, 1921 to 1923); explained in the lecture 'Composition with Twelve Tones', 1941
idea: Arnold Schoenberg's method of composing with twelve tones as a four-voice instrument. One row of all twelve pitch classes is laid out as the full 12 × 12 matrix of its 48 forms (prime, inversion, retrograde, retrograde inversion, at every transposition). Give each voice a form, cut its row into chords, scatter it across octaves and hear the aggregate (all twelve notes) complete, again and again, with no note given priority over another.
controls: 5 slots (four voices plus an aggregate bell); the row itself (swap notes, random row, all-interval row, four famous rows); for each of four voices: form (P, I, R, RI) and transposition, chosen by clicking the matrix, rhythm in 16ths, chord segmentation (single notes, dyads, trichords, tetrachords, hexachords), octave, register spread, rest chance, level and what happens at the end of a row (repeat, mirror, transpose by the row, random form); Klangfarben mode that passes the melody between instruments; a hexachordal combinatoriality finder that pairs voices so their hexachords complete aggregates; tempo, swing, reverb and echo.

title: Tide Predictor
source: Nature: the tide as a sum of cycles
author: William Thomson, Lord Kelvin (1824 to 1907), building on Laplace, with the harmonic analysis method developed by Kelvin and continued by George Darwin and Arthur Doodson
year: 1872 to 1873 (first tide-predicting machine); harmonic analysis of tides from the 1860s
idea: The tide at any harbour can be predicted as a sum of a few simple cycles set by the Moon and the Sun, each with its own period, size and timing. Kelvin's tide-predicting machine (1872 to 1873) added them with pulleys and a wire. Here each cycle (constituent) is a drone, the sum is a tide-gauge melody, and the slow swing between spring and neap tides is something you can hear: the lunar and solar drones beat against each other.
controls: 5 slots (gauge melody, constituent drones, high-water bell, low-water note, shore); eight tidal constituents (M2, S2, N2, K2, K1, O1, M4, M6), each with amplitude, phase and on/off; five illustrative coast types (semidiurnal, mixed, diurnal, shallow-water double tides, macrotidal); time speed (tidal hours per second); drone pitch, drones at true frequency ratios or tuned to the scale, breathing drones; gauge note rate, key, scale and range; high and low water sounds; shore level and how much the water opens the filter; reverb.

title: Plastic Unit
source: The Yellow Manifesto: notes for a manifesto
author: Victor Vasarely (1906 to 1997), Hungarian-French painter, father figure of Op Art
idea: Victor Vasarely's Yellow Manifesto (1955) as a grid sequencer built from 'plastic units': a square holding a contrasting inner form. Here the inner form is how a note is played, its pattern or colour is which of your samples plays it, and the grid is a 'plastic alphabet' you can permute, mirror, invert, multiply and bulge, as Vasarely did, so one small set of units makes endless variations.
controls: 5 slots (one per colour or pattern); a 16 × 8 grid of units (row = scale degree, column = 16th); six inner forms (circle, square, rhombus, tall ellipse, wide ellipse, dot) as six articulations; brush form and colour; key, scale, octave per colour; the Vega bulge (a moving lens that brightens and lengthens what it passes over) with size, speed and strength; negative mode (plays the outline of the empty space); mirror, retrograde, shift, permute colours, multiply a 4-step motif, generate with density; a 'programme' that applies a transformation every few bars; tempo, swing, reverb, echo; black-and-white or colour view.

title: USB Folder
source: Found-sound production: an ever-growing folder, and switching the lines round
author: Fred again.., with Jamie T on 'Lights Burn Dimmer'
idea: An ever-growing folder of tunes for rooms full of people, as an instrument. Cut a live vocal into its lines and switch their order round, stack three loops on house or garage drums, pick the room, then add the tune to your folder and let it roll from one track into the next.
controls: 8 slots (live vocal, three loops, kick, clap, hats, crowd); vocal cut at the gaps or into equal lines, a line order you build, switch, reverse and rotate, vocal isolation and pitch; three stacked loops with their own bar lengths, played as tempo-locked slices or varispeed; grooves (house, two-step, breakbeat, half-time), swing, sidechain pump, sub bass and progression; key and mode; five rooms (bedroom to arena) with crowd; intro, lines, build, drop and outro lengths with auto-arrange; the USB folder: add, load, delete, roll every N bars, make ten; optional Gemini room-to-track.

title: No Starting Point
source: Generative systems: the studio as compositional tool
author: Brian Eno
idea: In-studio composition, from the 1979 lecture 'The Studio as Compositional Tool', as an instrument. Start with an empty multitrack tape and no plan, put something on, put something else on, then take some of the original things off and see what you're left with. The mixing desk is the instrument: level, pan, echo, tone and tape speed per track, a bus compressor where pushing one sound up pushes the others down, and a brush to paint parts of the tape out.
controls: 6 slots (pad, piano, bass, bell, percussion, texture); a 12-track loop tape with cycle length, tempo, key and scale; PUT ON (any part type or a chosen one), TAKE OFF, TAKE A MIXTURE OFF, bring back, clear; per track: fader, pan, echo send, tone, tape speed (half, normal, double, backwards), mute, solo, erase; paint out or paint back on the tape; bus squash, echo time and feedback, space, tape hiss; mix drift and a 'gardener' that adds and subtracts by itself; MIDI overdub onto the selected track.

title: Tonality Diamond
source: Genesis of a Music: the Tonality Diamond and just intonation
author: Harry Partch (1901 to 1974), American composer, theorist and instrument builder
idea: Harry Partch's Tonality Diamond and his 43-tone just-intonation scale as a playable instrument. Every cell of the diamond is a pure ratio. Each row is an 'Otonality' (a chord built up from the overtones) and each column a 'Utonality' (its mirror image, built downwards). A walk pivots from one to the other through the note they share, while a gliding 'adapted viola' line slides between the 43 notes. A switch snaps everything to ordinary equal temperament so you can hear what is lost.
controls: 6 slots (diamond marimba, kithara, chromelodeon, adapted viola, cloud-chamber bowls, boo), all treated as pitched at C4; the diamond at the 5, 7, 9 or 11 limit; 1/1 pitch (G 392 Hz, as on Partch's instruments, or C or A); click a cell for a note or an edge label for a whole hexad; the pivot walk with beats per chord, meter (4, 5, 7 or 11), strum, density and glide; the 43-tone strip with cents and the difference from 12-ET; 12-ET compare; MIDI mapped to 43 steps an octave; levels per voice.

title: Dawn Syntax
source: The grammar of birdsong: syntax, the monotony threshold and the dawn chorus
author: Charles Hartshorne (1897 to 2000), philosopher and ornithologist; Kazuo Okanoya, on Bengalese finch song; Toshitaka Suzuki, David Wheatcroft and Michael Griesser, on Japanese tits
idea: Birdsong as grammar. Each bird cuts its sound into syllables and sings them through its own finite-state 'grammar': a table of which syllable may follow which, like the Bengalese finch songs studied by Kazuo Okanoya. Birds that repeat themselves rest longer between songs, after Charles Hartshorne's 'monotony threshold'. A dawn clock brings the chorus in bird by bird. A Japanese tit's call shows that order matters: ABC then D draws the flock in, while the same calls reversed barely gets a response, as in Toshitaka Suzuki's 2016 experiments.
controls: 6 slots (five birds and a dawn ambience); syllables cut at the gaps or into equal pieces, with a syllable count; an editable grammar table per bird (click a cell to change the weight); versatility (how often a bird changes its song) and the monotony pause; time of day with an automatic dawn and its length; free or pulsed rhythm, tempo, key, scale and pitch snapping; per-bird mute and pitch; the ABC–D and D–ABC calls; density, echo and space.

title: Merz Collage
source: Merz, and the equal evaluation of materials
author: Kurt Schwitters (1887 to 1948), German artist, poet and typographer from Hanover
idea: Kurt Schwitters's Merz as a sound collage. Tear fragments out of six materials (a tram ticket, newspaper, wood, wire, a voice and a piano) and glue them onto a page that loops. Across is time, up and down is pitch, size is loudness and the angle tilts the tone. EQUAL EVALUATION evens out every fragment's loudness, so no material outranks another, which is the principle of his 1919 text. The Merzbau mode keeps adding scraps, with older layers sinking under the new ones.
controls: 6 slots (ticket, newspaper, wood, wire/spring, voice, piano); click to glue a fragment of the chosen material, drag to move, wheel to tilt, Shift + wheel to resize, Shift + click to tear one off; TEAR (random fragment), tear length, equal evaluation, grid snap, key and scale for pitch snapping, loop bars and tempo; Merzbau growth with fade and a fragment limit; reverse and the 'Commerz → Merz' cut on the last fragment touched; echo, space and paper grit; optional Gemini: describe your found materials and get a collage.

title: Tube Brakes
source: Found-sound production: the auto-tuned found sound, and the room under every tune
author: Fred again..
idea: The ugly sound made beautiful: the screech of a braking tube train put through auto-tune, with the room it was recorded in quietly underneath. This is that method as an instrument. Load any found noise (a brake, a kettle, a door hinge, a gull, a squeaky trolley) and a pitch tracker follows it. A retuner snaps it to your key, either hard and robotic or gently, or makes it sing a riff or the chord tones. A room recording runs under everything through a phone-style squash that lifts the room, and house or two-step garage drums, pumping chords and an intro, build, drop and break arrangement sit on top.
controls: 6 slots (found sound, room tone, kick, clap, hats, keys); retune: mode (nearest note, chord tones, riff, MIDI), correction, retune speed, range, key and scale, harmony voices, time stretch, grain size, hook every N bars; room: level, phone squash, pump; drums: house or two-step, swing, density; chords: progression and style; arrangement auto or manual (intro, build, drop, break); reverb and delay; pitch-track display showing the raw and tuned lines.

title: Long Now Bells
source: January 07003: Bell Studies for the Clock of the Long Now
author: Brian Eno, with the Long Now Foundation (Danny Hillis, Stewart Brand and others)
idea: The album January 07003: Bell Studies for the Clock of the Long Now (2003) was research into the chimes for the Long Now Foundation's 10,000-year clock, which is meant to ring a different sequence of its ten bells every day. It started from English change ringing, where n bells are rung in every possible order without repeating one; ten bells give 10! (3,628,800) orders, roughly the number of days in 10,000 years. He also imagined bells with physical properties no real bell has. This instrument rings real change-ringing methods from place notation (rounds, plain hunt, Plain Bob, or your own notation), with a 'blue line' diagram tracing one bell. It also has a Long Now mode that gives every date its own permutation, so you can hear January 07003. The bells are additive (church, harmonic or enharmonic partials) and a STRETCH control bends them into imaginary metals; your own sample can be the bell.
controls: 4 slots (bell sample, hum drone, air, clock tick); method (rounds, plain hunt, Plain Bob, Grandsire-style custom place notation, Long Now day); bells 3 to 10; blow interval; handstroke gap; humanise; scale and key; partial set (church, fixed-ratio harmonic, enharmonic) with stretch, decay and brightness; synth and sample mix; drone and air levels; traced bell; Long Now year, month, day, repeats per day, auto-advance; reverb and delay; blue-line diagram and row list.

title: Gradus
source: Gradus ad Parnassum: the five species of counterpoint
author: Johann Joseph Fux (c. 1660 to 1741), court composer in Vienna
idea: For two centuries composers learned to write music from Johann Joseph Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum (1725). It teaches counterpoint in five 'species', each adding one new freedom: note against note, two against one, four against one, then tied syncopations, then florid writing. Every step has rules about consonance, motion and cadence. This instrument writes a fresh counterpoint to a cantus firmus (Fux's own D dorian tune, or a generated one) in species 1 to 4, above or below, in any of the six modes, and plays it with your sounds. You can also click to change any note and a rule checker tells you, live, which of Fux's rules you just broke and why. Each time round it can write a new line, move to the next mode or swap voices.
controls: 3 slots (cantus firmus voice, counterpoint voice, cadence bell); species 1 to 4; counterpoint above or below; mode (dorian, phrygian, lydian, mixolydian, aeolian, ionian); cantus: Fux's D dorian, or generate with a length; strictness (strict or relaxed); on each loop: repeat, new counterpoint, next mode, swap voices; tempo; transpose; articulation; humanise; reverb and delay; click-to-edit notes with live rule checking; interval figures.

title: Same River
source: Heraclitus: the river, the bow and lyre, the way up and down, the ever-living fire
author: Heraclitus of Ephesus (fl. c. 500 BC)
idea: Heraclitus of Ephesus (around 500 BC) left about a hundred fragments. The most famous says that upon those who step into the same rivers, other and other waters flow, so the river stays the same because its water never does. That is also a fair description of a loop in music. Here the riverbed (rhythm, melody, which sound plays where) repeats every pass, while a CURRENT moves the point each hit reads from in your samples, so every pass is the same pattern made of different water. EROSION lets the bed itself change slowly. Three more fragments shape the rest. The road up and the road down are one and the same: a melody that turns into its own inversion. A harmony that turns back on itself, as of the bow and the lyre: two strings pulled out of tune and back. An ever-living fire, kindled and quenched in measures: density that grows and dies in bar-length measures. (Fragments in our own translation; public domain.)
controls: 5 slots (river water, second water, stone, lyre string, fire); current (how far the read point moves each pass), Cratylus mode (new water on every hit), erosion (how much the riverbed changes each pass), steps and bars, density; way up and down: river, way up / way down (alternating inversion), circle (palindrome); bow and lyre: tension (cents), turning period, lyre level; fire: measures, depth, crackle; high and low (octave spread); key and scale; tempo; reverb and delay; new riverbed.

title: Pop Art Is
source: Pop Art is: a 1957 letter defining popular art
author: Richard Hamilton (1922 to 2011), British artist and member of the Independent Group
idea: In January 1957 Richard Hamilton wrote to two architect friends with a definition of 'Pop Art'. He meant the popular culture of adverts, films, cars and records, not yet the gallery art that later took the name. The definition was eleven words long: Popular, Transient, Expendable, Low cost, Mass produced, Young, Witty, Sexy, Gimmicky, Glamorous, Big business. This instrument is a pop-song factory driven by those eleven words. Each one is a giant typographic fader that changes the music: Transient sets how short each song is, Expendable how completely the next one forgets it, Low cost crushes the bits, Mass produced stacks copies of the hook, Big business squashes the master and stamps a jingle on the end. Songs are generated, sold and replaced one after another. Hamilton also doubted whether such art could be sincere, so there is a SINCERITY? knob too. An optional Gemini panel writes a jingle for any product you describe.
controls: 6 slots (hook voice, kick, clap, hats, bass/keys, gimmick); eleven characteristic faders (drag the words, or keys 1 to 9, 0 and -); sincerity?; key and major/minor; base tempo; hook, drums, bass and pad levels; new song, jingle now; Gemini jingle writer (optional, using your own key); chart of past songs fading as they are forgotten; units-sold counter.

title: Emotional Frameworks
source: Found-sound production: one vocal line in many emotional frameworks
author: Fred again.., with advice from Brian Eno
idea: One vocal line, many emotional frameworks: build loads of versions around a single line to hear what the same words become in different settings. Add a rule passed on from Brian Eno (start each piece from a random sketch you have no control over), keep fragments of old sketches to bring back later, and put reverb on the whole master. This instrument does all four with your own sounds. One vocal line in slot 1 runs through seven frameworks: lifted house, two-step, numb, panic in the club, gospel, a peak-time rave and a slow, meditative space. Each version has an intro, a build, a drop and a break, and VERSIONS mode keeps making new ones so you can hear what the same words become.
controls: 8 slots (vocal line, second voice, kick, clap, hats, keys, room, sketch); seven frameworks with their own tempo, chords, drums, keys and space; phrase or chop vocal, vocal pitch, how often it sings, chop density; second voice call and response through a night-out chain; build length, drop power, sidechain pump, swing; random sketch you have no control over (draws from a folder) with slow-down; REMEMBER and RECALL a fragment; reverb on the master; versions log; Gemini turns a described day into a framework (optional, your own key).

title: Lantern Marsh
source: Ambient 4: On Land (sleeve notes)
author: Brian Eno
idea: Ambient 4: On Land (1982) is music made partly from non-instruments (chains, sticks, stones) and from old tapes reworked into new music, which its sleeve notes compare to composting. The sounds live their own lives at a distance, some beyond hearing, so the listener stands inside a landscape where foreground and background are no longer separate. Lantern Marsh is a map you walk across. Eight sources (your sounds, or built-in chain, sticks, stones, rooks, frogs, insects, a drone and a far bell) each keep their own irregular time. Where you stand decides what you hear: distance sets level, darkness, width and reverb. COMPOST turns the last few seconds of the landscape into a slow bed of new sound.
controls: 8 source slots plus a compost slot; drag sources and the listener on the map; per source on/off and its own period; earshot radius, distance darkness, distance reverb, foreground/background flatten; tape speed and wow (time distortion); sources wander and the listener walks; compost: capture the landscape and replay it as slow grains, auto compost; ten place presets named after On Land tracks.

title: In C, Your Way
source: In C (1964), with its performing directions
author: Terry Riley
idea: In C (1964, premiered at the San Francisco Tape Music Center in November 1964) gives a group of any size 53 short melodic patterns and a few rules. Each player works through the patterns in order and repeats each one as many times as they like, so the parts slide against each other, and a steady pulse of eighth notes on high C holds everything together. The rules matter more than the notes: don't hurry, stay within two or three patterns of each other, drop out and listen, and meet in unison at least once or twice. This instrument puts those rules on sliders for up to twelve players, using your sounds. Its 53 cells are its own, written to follow the broad harmonic path of the piece (C, then a turn towards G with F sharp, then B flat near the end). You can edit any cell or write a new set from a seed.
controls: 8 slots (pulse plus seven player timbres, all tuned to C4); players 2 to 12; how long each player stays on a cell (min and max repeats); how far apart players may drift (spread); drop-out chance; rhythmic shifts; augmentation; octave spread; dynamics; pulse level and on/off; a seed that writes a new set of 53 cells; a cell editor; unison, ending and restart.

title: Zeno's Race
source: The paradoxes of motion
author: Zeno of Elea (c. 490 to c. 430 BC), as reported and answered by Aristotle
year: c. 450 BC (Zeno); Aristotle's Physics, 4th century BC
idea: Zeno of Elea argued that motion is impossible. Before you reach a goal you must first reach the half-way point, then half of what is left, forever. Swift Achilles can never catch the tortoise, because he must first reach the place the tortoise has just left. A flying arrow, at any instant, is simply where it is, so it is at rest. And in the stadium, a body seems to pass something in half the time it takes to pass something else. We know these arguments mainly through Aristotle's Physics, which also answers them: time, like distance, can be divided without end, and infinitely many shrinking steps can add up to a finite time. This instrument turns each paradox into a musical process. The Z switch flips between Zeno's view (steps that never arrive, an arrow frozen at every moment) and Aristotle's (the steps add up, the riser lands, Achilles overtakes).
controls: 8 slots (half-way voice, goal hit, tortoise, Achilles, arrow texture, three stadium rows); ZENO or ARISTOTLE view (Z); level for each paradox; dichotomy race length and target interval; Achilles' speed ratio, the tortoise's head start, melody scale and root; arrow moment size, hold, flight speed; stadium speed and frame of reference (still row or moving row); drone.

title: Make Way for Magic
source: Refus global
author: Paul-Émile Borduas and fifteen co-signatories (the Automatistes), including Jean-Paul Riopelle, Claude Gauvreau, Marcelle Ferron, Fernand Leduc and Françoise Sullivan
idea: Refus global (Total Refusal) was published in Montreal on 9 August 1948 by the painter Paul-Émile Borduas and fifteen other Automatistes, among them Jean-Paul Riopelle, Marcelle Ferron, Françoise Sullivan, Fernand Leduc and Claude Gauvreau. Four hundred copies were printed. It rejected the closed, fearful society of Duplessis-era Quebec and called for art made by automatism: gestures that come before conscious intention. Its most famous lines are a list of what to make way for: magic, objective mysteries, love and necessity. Here you paint gestures and the gestures play. Left to right is time, height is pitch and the speed of your hand is how loud and bright it is. There are four layers, one for each 'Place à', four brushes (Riopelle-like dabs, lines, splashes and Gauvreau-like syllables), an automatic hand that paints by itself, REFUS to wipe everything and RESPONSABILITÉ to keep what you choose.
controls: 8 slots (magic, objective mysteries, love, necessity, syllables voice, splash texture, ground, refusal crash); paint with four brushes on four layers; loop length; scale, root and pitch range; automatic hand (rate and wildness); strokes fade unless kept; REFUS wipes, RESPONSABILITÉ keeps, undo; play-as-you-paint; ground level; Gemini paints strokes from a sentence (optional, your own key).

title: Pavement Garage
source: Found-sound production: the field recording as the drum kit and the chords
author: Inspired by found-sound house and garage producers of the 2020s (for example Fred again..), and by UK garage
design_credit: Risograph zine printing (DIY self-publishing, 1990s to now)
idea: Turn a field recording into the band. Its own clatter is cut out and layered under house and garage drums, its hiss is tuned into the chords by a bank of resonators, and a phone voice memo is chopped into an emotional hook on top. A journal of four pages, one recording and one line of writing each, builds to a euphoric drop and then lets the street back in. Found-sound dance producers of the 2020s work this way: phone audio, field recordings and journal-like sampling over two-step and four-to-the-floor drums.
controls: 8 slots (voice memo, field recording A, field recording B, kick, clap, hats, keys, sub); groove (two-step garage, four-to-the-floor house, speed-garage bassline, broken), swing, tempo, key; FIELD KIT (the field recording's own hits layered on the drums, sorted low, mid and high); TUNED STREET (six resonators tuned to the chord tones); phone-ness of the voice; a 16-step chop lane you click; chop pitch and density; page length, build bars, euphoria and key lift for the drop; four journal pages (a line of writing, a progression and a field recording each); VJ full-screen mode.

title: Return Time
source: Generative tape loops: unequal lengths, your own cards, the studio as instrument
source_short: Unequal tape loops and the return time
author: Inspired by Brian Eno's ambient and generative working methods
design_credit: Ulm functionalist product design: the Braun and Ulm School of Design approach (Dieter Rams, Hans Gugelot and colleagues)
idea: Tape loops of different lengths never quite line up, so a few simple phrases keep making new combinations, and the moment they all return together can be days or centuries away. This machine runs six loops of unequal length, four of notes and two of your own trimmed sounds, and works out exactly when they will next meet. Each loop is a channel of an imaginary tape studio with its own speed, wear, wow and echo, so the studio itself is the instrument. You write your own prompt cards, the machine draws one every few minutes and acts on it, a gardener lets worn loops fade and plants new ones, and an attention fader moves the music between something to listen to closely and something to leave in the background.
controls: 6 slots (piano, voice pad, glass, low tone, tape loop A, tape loop B); four note loops with their own length (3 to 40 s), speed, level and phrase; two audio tape loops whose length is the trimmed region (drag S and E); return-time readout (when all six loops line up again) and meetings counter; attention fader from IGNORE to LISTEN; tape wear per pass, wow and flutter, saturation, tape echo; gardener on/off and rate; scale and key; density; your own prompt cards (one per line, optional [action] tag), drawn by hand or every N minutes; Gemini writes new cards from a mood (optional, your own key).

title: Circle Walk
source: The circle of fifths: keys, relative minors and progressions by fifths
author: Nikolai Diletskii's Grammatika (1679) and Johann David Heinichen's Der General-Bass in der Composition (1728); the Pythagorean comma (ancient Greek tuning theory)
year: 1679 and 1728 (circle diagrams); about 500 BC onwards (the comma)
design_credit: Googie: mid-century coffee-shop and space-age roadside architecture and signage of Southern California
idea: Arrange the twelve keys in a circle where each step is a perfect fifth and the whole of Western harmony becomes a map: neighbouring keys share all but one note, relative minors share a key signature, and the strongest chord progressions move round the circle one fifth at a time. This instrument walks that map with your own sounds. Pick a walk (the diatonic chain of falling fifths, two-five-one chains, a tour of all twelve dominants, or a pivot-chord modulation to a neighbouring key) and hear every chord voice-led to the next by the smallest moves. Switch to pure fifths and the circle stops closing: after twelve perfect fifths you arrive about a quarter of a semitone sharp, the gap that equal temperament spreads around the circle.
controls: 7 slots (keys C4, bass C2, lead C5, pad C4, kick, hat, snare/rim); four walks (falling fifths in the key, ii-V-I chains, the twelve-dominant tour, pivot modulation); key (on the circle) and major or relative minor; modulate after each lap (stay, flatwards, sharpwards, to a random neighbour); sevenths or triads; harmonic-minor V; chord length; equal or pure-fifth tuning with drift readout and comma reset; groove (bossa, brushes, four, none); swing; guide-tone melody amount; keys, bass, lead, pad and drum levels.

title: Mycelial Network
source: Mycelial networks: the fungal web beneath a forest
author: Inspired by research on mycorrhizal fungi and fungal growth
design_credit: Arts and Crafts private-press printing: the Kelmscott Press of William Morris (1891 to 1898)
idea: Under a forest floor, fungal threads branch, fuse and wrap the roots of the trees, trading minerals and water for sugar, so the forest is joined by a living network you never see. This instrument grows one. Five trees are five of your sounds; threads grow out from them, branch and fuse where they meet, and once two trees are joined a pulse sent from one reaches the other after a delay set by the length of the path. The network becomes the score: rhythms come from distances, a well-fed web fruits into mushrooms that ring out as chords, and drought makes it die back to silence.
controls: 7 slots (five trees: bell, wood, low string, voice, pluck; forest floor grains; fruiting chime); growth rate, branching, fusion distance; drought (die-back) and FEED (a growth burst); pulse speed along the threads, reach, how often the trees pulse (mother tree only, or every tree on its own period), relay chance (a tree that receives a pulse sends its own); hum of the branch points (grains); fruiting threshold; scale and key; quantise to the grid or free time; levels; click to drop a spore or fire a tree.

title: Regulating Lines
source: Purism: After Cubism (1918)
author: Amédée Ozenfant and Charles-Édouard Jeanneret (later known as Le Corbusier)
design_credit: The mid-century paperback cover grid: Romek Marber's grid for Penguin crime and Pelican covers (1961)
idea: After the fragments of Cubism, a 1918 Paris manifesto asked for an art of order: plain standard objects such as bottles, glasses, pipes and guitars, perfected by use like good machines, arranged on regulating lines of exact proportion and painted in a calm, ranked scale of colours. This instrument makes that still life playable. Six standard objects are six of your sounds; where you place each one on the canvas sets when it plays, how high it is sets its pitch and how wide sets how long it lasts. Regulating lines (halves, thirds, the golden section or the square root of two) pull every object into proportion, objects that share a contour sound together, and the colour scale decides each object's character.
controls: 7 slots (bottle, glass, pipe, guitar, jug C2, plate, machine pulse); drag objects to move them (they snap to the regulating lines), drag the right edge to change length; four proportion systems (halves, thirds, golden section, root two); snap on or off; marriage of contours (overlapping objects play together); constants (married objects tuned to unisons, fourths and fifths); colour scale per object (the calm major scale, the dynamic scale, the transitional scale); canvas length in beats; tempo; key and scale; legato; the hand (human timing) versus the machine; machine pulse level; ORDER snaps everything, SCATTER throws it into cubist disorder.

title: Resample Chain
source: Found-sound production: the resample chain
author: Inspired by found-audio house and garage producers of the 2020s (no quotes, no copied patterns or audio)
year: 2020s, from older sampling and tape-bounce practice
design_credit: Cassette J-card and home-made mixtape inlay design
idea: A phone voice memo, a street recording and a few drums become a house or garage track in five sections: intro, verse, build, drop and break. The twist is the bounce. At the end of every section the instrument records its own mix into a ninth slot, and the next section chops that bounce instead of (or as well as) the original memo, so each pass is a copy of a copy: warmer, darker and more like a tape you carried around. A snare roll, a rising riser and a deliberate one-beat gap lead into a drop built from your own vocal chops, tuned to the chords. Everything is editable and every sound is yours.
controls: 9 slots (voice memo, room or street, kick, clap, hat, chord stab, bass, riser, bounce); five sections with adjustable length, jump or hold; groove (four-to-the-floor, two-step garage, broken); tempo, swing, key and chord loop; sample root so chops are tuned to the chords; chop density, chop length and tuning mode; hook re-roll; bounce mix (how much comes from the bounce), copy wear (how much each pass darkens) and auto-bounce; sidechain pump; build roll and gap; levels for drums, chords, bass, chops and room; VJ cassette-reel visuals.

title: Learned Garden
source: Generative systems: gardening, not architecture
author: Inspired by generative-music practice since the 1990s, and by Andrey Markov's chains of probabilities (1906 to 1913)
year: 1990s to now; Markov chains from 1906 to 1913
design_credit: Mid-century seed packets and nursery catalogue illustration
idea: Plant a short phrase and a garden of independent players learns its habits: which note tends to follow which. Each plant then wanders through that map at its own pace, so the music never repeats but always sounds like its seed. You tend it rather than build it: water it with your own notes and it learns your habits, let it feed on itself and it slowly settles into favourite paths, let a few weeds in and it surprises you, prune it back and it forgets. A slow season cycle thins and thickens the garden over minutes, and an attention fader moves it between music to listen to and music to ignore.
controls: 7 slots (pluck, bell, pad, low voice, texture, seed drop, your hand); seed phrase (scale degrees you can type); key and scale; learned transition map (first or second order memory); temperature (how adventurous); weeds; habit (how much it learns from itself); plant and prune plants; speed; season length in minutes or a fixed season; attention (ignore to listen); your notes on the keyboard, the map or MIDI teach it; levels for plants, pad, your hand and texture.

title: Song Form Blocks
source: Song form: the blues, AABA and verse-chorus, with the hook and call and response
author: Anonymous folk and popular traditions; the blues of the early 1900s; the popular song of the 1920s to 1950s
year: Early 1900s to 1950s (blues); 1920s to 1950s (AABA); 1950s to now (verse and chorus)
design_credit: Nineteenth-century wood-type posters and playbills (American letterpress job printing)
idea: Most songs are built from a handful of blocks. The twelve-bar blues is a three-line chord pattern that has carried countless songs. AABA is a thirty-two-bar form: a tune twice, a contrasting bridge, the tune again. Verse and chorus put a talking section against a singing one. This instrument lets you pick a form and see it as a row of printed blocks, then plays it with your own sounds: a band (keys, bass, drums), a hook that you can re-roll, and a call-and-response conversation in which one voice makes a short phrase and another answers it. Change the form, the swing or the way the answer is made and you hear how structure shapes feeling.
controls: 8 slots (keys, bass, kick, snare or brush, ride or hat, caller, responder, organ); five forms (12-bar blues, minor 12-bar, 8-bar blues, 32-bar AABA, verse-chorus-bridge); key, tempo and swing from straight to shuffle; chord richness (triads, sevenths, ninths); quick change and turnaround for the blues; comping style (stabs, sustained, charleston, shuffle); bass style (walking, root and fifth, boogie); note set (minor blues, major blues, major); hook strength and length; call length (one or two bars) and answer style (echo, mirror, fifth above, resolve, free); blue-note bend; levels; VJ chord blocks.

title: Standing Waves
source: Standing waves and the harmonic series
author: Physics and the acoustics of strings, pipes and plates
year: Ancient observation; plates studied from the late 1700s
design_credit: Natural-history plates and scientific engraving (the printed 'Fig. 1' page)
idea: Every pitched sound that rings is made of a stack of pure tones whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of a lowest one: the harmonic series. A string, a pipe and a voice all behave this way, and the series gives us the octave, the fifth, the major third and the strange, flat seventh. This instrument makes the series audible. A bank of sixteen ringing filters is tuned to the multiples of a low note. Your own sounds are fed through it, so they ring like a struck plate. A melody walks up and down the series in pure, just tuning. On the screen a plate of sand shows the pattern each tone would draw, and you can switch tones on and off and make the plate stiffer so the tones drift out of tune.
controls: 6 slots (melody voice, strike, bow or breath, drone, tick, bell); sixteen resonators with a clickable spectrum (click or drag the bars to set how loudly each harmonic rings); fundamental note; resonance (Q); stiffness (how far the tones are pushed sharp, as in a real stiff string or plate); spectral tilt; excitation sends from the melody, a strike pattern and a continuous bow; melody range and density; fundamental movement (stay, up a fifth, down a fourth, walk the series); just or equal tuning; levels; VJ sand-plate view.

title: Zero Field
source: ZERO: the countdown, the zone of silence and the new beginning
author: A group of artists founded in Düsseldorf in 1957
design_credit: The broadcast test card (television test patterns, 1950s to 1970s)
idea: In the late 1950s a group of artists in Düsseldorf took the name ZERO. They borrowed it from the countdown before a rocket launch, and from the idea of a zone of silence from which something new can begin. Their work favoured light, vibration, repetition and pure, quiet structure over expression and story. This instrument turns that attitude into sound. Seven repeating voices of your own sounds make a calm, even field. A countdown removes them one by one, down to zero, where only a single quiet tone and silence remain. Then the field begins again, perhaps in a new key. Small controls let the voices drift out of step, wobble in pitch like light on a surface, or lock tightly in time.
controls: 8 slots (pulse, click, hat, tone A, tone B, shimmer, voice, and a zero tone that plays in the silence); countdown length and stage length in beats; zone-of-silence length; direction (down, up, or both) and what happens at restart (same key, up a fifth, random); pulse pattern sets (locked, moire, sparse); drift between voices; pitch vibration depth and speed; path length (how many different notes each voice cycles through); note set (one note, pentatonic, major, whole-tone); brightness filter; stereo width; accent; row mutes (click the colour bars); levels for every voice; VJ test-card view.
